summary: For ages 11–13, this concept builds understanding of radiometric dating: a radioactive parent isotope decays to a daughter with a characteristic, constant half-life, so the parent:daughter RATIO in a sample yields an absolute age. Key ideas: half-life = time for half the parent to decay; after n half-lives the parent fraction = (1/2)^n; dating reads how far decay has run, not a stopwatch from a known start; and the isotope-clock must be matched to the age range (carbon-14 ~5,730 yr half-life, organic, useful to ~50,000 yr; uranium-lead / potassium-argon for millions-to-billions of years, igneous rock). The core activity is a manipulable decay model; strong companions are a ratio/age computation task and a clock-matching question; a static annotated decay curve and a scientist dialogue address specific aspects (pattern reading and the 'why date the ash, not the bone' misconception) as supporting scaffolds.
misconceptions: 'You can carbon-date dinosaur bones' — C-14's ~50,000-year range is far too short for 66-million-year fossils.
'Radiometric dating counts down from when the animal died like a stopwatch' — it reads the parent:daughter ratio of a decay process.
'After two half-lives everything has decayed' — a quarter of the parent remains; decay is exponential, never reaching zero cleanly.
'We date the fossil itself' — usually the surrounding volcanic rock is dated, bracketing the fossil's age.
'Half-life changes with conditions' — it is essentially constant, which is what makes it a reliable clock.

activities.title: Wind the radioactive clock: halving and solving for age
steps: Start with a grid of 'parent' atoms and advance a time-slider; watch atoms flip to a 'daughter' colour as a half-life counter ticks.
Before advancing, predict what fraction of parent will remain after 1, 2, and 3 half-lives, then check against the grid and a parent:daughter ratio bar.
Connect the pattern to the formula: parent fraction = (1/2)^n after n half-lives (1/2, then 1/4, then 1/8).

Switch to 'mystery sample' mode: given a measured parent:daughter ratio such as 1 part parent to 3 parts daughter, and assuming the sample started with no daughter and nothing has been added or lost since, work out how many half-lives have passed (here, two — one quarter of the parent remains) and estimate the age using the half-life.
Use a clock-picker to choose the right isotope system for a given material and age (e.g. carbon-14 for recent organic material; uranium-lead for a 100-million-year rock).

Try to carbon-date a dinosaur bone and observe the result: too little original carbon-14 left to measure, because dinosaur fossils are at least 66 million years old, far beyond carbon-14's ~50,000-year range; then switch to uranium-lead on a bracketing volcanic layer.
activities.insight: Dating is not a stopwatch started at a known moment — it reads how far a decay with a known, constant half-life has run via the parent:daughter ratio, and the clock's half-life must match the age being measured. The number of atoms decaying per unit time is not constant; it falls as the parent is depleted, because each half-life removes half of whatever parent remains.

activities.title: Compute the age and match the clock
steps: Given a parent:daughter ratio and a half-life, set or write the number of half-lives and the approximate age (e.g. one quarter of parent left and a 1.3-billion-year half-life → two half-lives → ~2.6 billion years).

Answer which isotope system would date a stated material: e.g. which clock for a 100-million-year igneous rock (uranium-lead or potassium-argon), and which for a few-thousand-year-old piece of wood or bone (carbon-14).
Order a set of samples from youngest to oldest from their parent:daughter ratios (more daughter relative to parent = older, for the same isotope).
activities.insight: Once the decay model is understood, the parent:daughter ratio and half-life give a calculable age, and the appropriate isotope depends on both the material and the timescale.

activities.title: Read the decay curve
steps: Examine an annotated exponential half-life decay curve and reveal the marked points at 50% (one half-life), 25% (two), and 12.5% (three).
At each point, state the elapsed number of half-lives and the fraction of parent remaining.
Describe in words why the curve flattens and never reaches exactly zero.
activities.insight: The decay pattern is exponential: equal time intervals each remove half of what remains, so the fraction keeps halving rather than falling linearly to zero.

activities.title: Ask the geochronologist: why not carbon-date a T. rex?
steps: Pose the question 'Why can't you carbon-date a dinosaur bone?' and read or discuss the explanation.
Explore the follow-up: why scientists usually date volcanic ash layers above and below a fossil rather than the fossil itself.
Summarise in their own words what is actually being dated and why the choice of isotope matters.
activities.insight: Carbon-14's ~50,000-year range is far too short for 66-million-year fossils, and fossils are typically dated by bracketing igneous/ash layers whose minerals suit long-lived isotope systems.

checkQuestion: A friend says: 'We can find out how old a dinosaur bone is by carbon-dating it, the same way we date ancient wood or mummies.' Is that right? Explain what radiometric dating measures and why the method matters here.
checkAnswer: No. Carbon-14 has a short half-life and is only useful up to roughly 50,000 years, but non-avian dinosaurs are around 66+ million years old — any carbon-14 would have decayed away long ago. Dinosaur-age rock is dated with long-lived isotopes like uranium-lead or potassium-argon. Radiometric dating works by measuring the ratio of parent to daughter isotope: since the parent decays with a known half-life, the ratio gives an absolute age.
